source.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
source.authors: Alethea Power; Yuri Burda; Harrison Edwards; Igor Babuschkin; Vedant Misra

record.file_problem: None noted. The text includes figure captions and descriptions, but the plotted values themselves are not present.
record.tranche_reason: This is the original study of delayed generalization on small algorithmic datasets, using training and validation accuracy over optimization time and training-set sizes.
record.gate_note: The study reports direct results on delayed generalization and dataset-size effects. It also reports optimizer comparisons and generalization failures; results cited from other work are not included. The paper calls the held-out split a validation set, not a test set.
record.test_reason: This is an original source for V1. It trains small transformers on binary-operation tables and tracks training and validation accuracy over steps and training fractions. It also reports weight-decay ablations relevant to V5. Because it is an original source, it gets no verdict labels.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also say late generalization was typical only near the minimal dataset size that generalizes within budget, and that curves track each other at larger sizes. They also find optimization noise helps, and conjecture that grokking relates to finding flatter minima.
record.recipe_differences: This is the original study, using a small transformer trained on random subsets of binary-operation tables and tracking training and validation performance.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization depends on task and training-set size; optimizer and regularization choices affect data efficiency. Learning rate must be tuned within a relatively narrow window for generalization to occur.

fits_no_version.finding: Sharpness of the found minimum correlates with validation accuracy across S5 seeds (Spearman −0.795, p<0.000014).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking coincides with reaching flatter regions of the loss landscape.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding up to 1000 random-label outliers barely affects data efficiency; larger numbers shrink the range of data fractions that generalize.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization on algorithmic tasks is robust to a small number of memorized outliers.

fits_no_version.finding: t-SNE plots of output-layer weights show the structure of the mathematical objects (circles for modular addition, cosets for S5); this is more apparent with weight decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalizing networks learn embeddings reflecting the task's algebraic structure.

record.problems: The supplied text does not include the plotted curves or their individual values. Many results are summarized qualitatively; the study reports three seeds for most experiments and seven for the learning-time curves, but gives no uncertainty intervals for the key grokking timings.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the Figure 2 optimizer/data-efficiency curve values, Figure 2 operation-by-operation best validation accuracies, or Figure 6 outlier results: the supplied text gives captions or qualitative summaries but omits plotted values, and the outlier experiment does not report the delayed-generalization timing named by V1.

untested.parts: No circuit formation, Fourier algorithm or mechanistic progress measures. The t-SNE embeddings are qualitative and taken at the end of training only.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep.
No test of an efficient circuit displacing memorization, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
No comparison of the algorithms found across runs.
No test of optimizer instability or floating-point softmax artifacts. Optimizer variants are compared only for data efficiency.

missing.what: Validation loss rises from about 10^2 to about 10^5 steps before a second descent: a loss-curve view of the delay.
Training accuracy reaches 100% after 10^3–10^4 updates for all optimizer variants; some generalization occurs even without weight decay at high data fractions.
Learning rate must be tuned within about one order of magnitude for generalization to occur.

record.verdict_notes: This is an original source for V1 (and the origin of the weight-decay observation), so no verdict labels are given. The held-out split is called a validation set. The record's numbers lost their superscripts (10^n was rendered as '10n').

versions.untested_parts: The key curves use validation rather than test accuracy. The study tests small algorithmic operation-table tasks, not every kind of algorithmic dataset.
No gradual formation or removal of circuits, Fourier algorithm, or continuous mechanistic progress measure is tested.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale sweep, weight-norm transition, or lazy-to-rich transition is tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.

The study compares weight-decay settings and data efficiency, but does not test whether an efficient generalizing circuit displaces memorization, or the proposed critical dataset size and ungrokking predictions.
The study does not compare identifiable algorithms across runs or test whether runs converge to the same algorithm.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point softmax artifact is tested or controlled as a hypothesis.

rows.subject: small transformer trained on modular division mod 97
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads; about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Train on a random subset of the modular-division operation table and track training accuracy over optimization steps.
rows.value: Training accuracy becomes close to perfect at < 103 optimization steps.
rows.note: The figure's curve is described in the text; no exact accuracy value is given.
rows.check: Superscripts were lost: '106' means 10^6 steps and '< 103' means < 10^3. Otherwise correct. Adam with no weight decay and a 10^6 budget match Appendix A.1.2.

source_check.correct: Training accuracy becomes close to perfect before 10^3 optimization steps. Training budget: 10^6 steps; Adam without weight decay; 50% training data.
source_check.problem: Lost superscripts render the training time and budget incorrectly as 103 and 106.

rows.operation_detail: Train on a random subset of the modular-division operation table and track validation accuracy over optimization steps.

rows.subject: small transformer on abstract group S5 product
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads; about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Vary the fraction of the operation table used for training and measure optimization time to reach validation accuracy thresholds.
rows.measure: optimization steps until validation accuracy first exceeds 99%
rows.value: In the vicinity of 25–30% of data, a decrease of 1% of training data leads to an increase of 40–50% in median time to generalization.
rows.locator: Section 3.1.1; Figure 1 center description; Appendix A.1.2
rows.note: The text reports the change in median time but not the individual times at each data fraction.
rows.check: The budget condition is missing. Section 3.1.1 used 5·10^5 steps with the default AdamW (weight decay 1), per Appendix A.1.2.

source_check.correct: Near 25–30% training data, a 1% decrease in training data increases median generalization time by 40–50%. Additional conditions: 5 × 10^5 optimization steps; default AdamW with learning rate 10^-3 and weight decay 1; seven random seeds.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1.1, paragraph describing Figure 1 center; Appendix A.1.2.
source_check.problem: Stated conditions are correct, but the row omits the optimization budget and optimizer.

rows.subject: small transformer on abstract group S5 product
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads; about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Vary training dataset size and measure time until training accuracy first reaches 99%.
rows.measure: optimization steps until training accuracy first reaches 99%
rows.value: Generally trends down as dataset size decreases and stays in the range of 103–104 optimization steps.
rows.note: This is contrasted in the text with the rapidly increasing time to validation generalization.
rows.check: Superscripts were lost (10^3–10^4). This is a supporting contrast row: training time does not grow as data shrinks.

rows.subject: small transformers on the binary operations studied
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads; about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Describe training and validation behavior for dataset sizes near the minimum at which the network generalizes within the allotted budget.

conditions.value: near the minimum for generalization within the allotted optimization budget

rows.measure: training and validation accuracy over optimization
rows.baseline: validation accuracy at chance level before generalization
rows.value: The authors say the behaviors were typical for all binary operations at these dataset sizes; for larger datasets, training and validation curves tend to track more closely.
rows.note: This is an aggregate statement across the studied operations, not a separate result for each operation.
rows.check: Could add the Section 3.1.1 statement that the exponential rise in time to generalization was seen on all tasks that generalized.

rows.subject: small transformer on x3 + xy2 + y (mod 97)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads; about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Train at varying fractions of the operation table and assess whether the model generalizes within the optimization budget.
rows.value: The task did not lead to generalization within the allowed optimization budget at any percentage of data up to 95%; converged models effectively memorized the training dataset.
rows.note: A stated counterexample to generalization within the budget on one of the algorithmic operations studied.
rows.check: This is the budget condition for the default runs (10^5 steps, AdamW), not 'not stated'. It is a no-generalization case, not a delayed one.

rows.subject: small transformer on abstract group S5 product
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads; about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimizer and regularization variants on data efficiency.
rows.value: Adding weight decay has a very large effect on data efficiency, more than halving the amount of samples needed compared to most other interventions.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison; the figure's precise values are not present in the supplied text.
rows.check: This bears only on the weight-decay-helps part of V5. No circuit, norm, critical dataset size or ungrokking is measured. The baseline 'most other interventions' is a comparison among Figure 2 left variants at a 10^5 budget.

rows.subject: small transformer on abstract group S5 product
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads; about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compare weight decay toward initialization with weight decay toward the origin.
rows.value: Weight decay toward the initialization is effective, but not quite as effective as weight decay toward the origin.
rows.note: No circuit or norm mechanism is measured.
rows.check: This compares two weight-decay targets. 'Partial' is not meaningful against V5's effect. The authors read it as the zero-weight prior explaining 'part, but not all' of weight decay's benefit.
